88% of VC-backed founders walk away with $0 at exit.

A working paper by researchers at Wharton and the University of Zurich tracked 248,454 founders across 157,669 US venture-backed companies between 1987 and 2025.

Here's what they found:

-- 88% of founders received zero at exit.

-- The top 1% of founders captured 79% of total founder exit value.

-- Among the 12% who received something, the median after-tax payout was $4.8 million.

There's a bigger problem hiding in these numbers.

Venture capital is built around power-law returns.

Investors need a handful of enormous outcomes to generate returns for their funds.

Which means you can build a genuinely good business, have paying customers, meaningful revenue and a strong product, and still not have the kind of company your investors need you to build.

This is where founders can get stuck.

The business is real. But it isn't growing fast enough to attract the next round, and a modest acquisition might not make sense to the people sitting above you on the cap table.

So you keep chasing growth. Keep raising. Keep betting more years on the possibility that the company will eventually become 10x bigger.

And sometimes that's absolutely the right bet.

If you're building a venture-backed company, you should take your shot at building something generational.

But what happens when you realise it isn't going to be that company?

I think the venture ecosystem needs better options for founders who have built good businesses that simply don't fit the traditional venture model.

That's the gap Rohit Mittal and the team at Helium Ventures are trying to fill.

Helium acquires and stewards software businesses that have real customers and product-market fit, but no longer fit the traditional venture growth model.

The goal is to give founders a clean exit while giving the business, its team and its customers a future.

If you're a founder in this position, reach out to @rohitdotmittal or @heliumventureco.

And if you know a founder who's stuck between raising another round, grinding it out, or shutting down a good business, tag them below or DM me privately. I'll gladly make an introduction to Rohit.

A good business deserves a future, even if it never becomes a unicorn.

IPXExchange has an important challenge to solve if it wants to bring real intellectual property onchain: making ownership and usage rights clear.

Take a music project as an example.

A single song can involve a composer, lyricist, vocalist, producer and record label. The person who creates the music may not own every commercial right attached to it.

Now imagine bringing that project into an onchain system.

Before tokenization becomes meaningful, several questions need answers:

1. Who legally owns the original intellectual property?

2. Which rights can actually be represented by the token?

3. Can supporters receive commercial benefits, or are they only participating in a funding arrangement?

4. What happens if the creator has already licensed the same content elsewhere?

5. Who handles disputes when ownership is challenged?

This is where I think @IPXExchange has an opportunity to build something more meaningful than a simple token marketplace.

Its vision of connecting IP tokenization, creator funding, milestone-based escrow and content distribution needs a clear legal foundation underneath.

Blockchain can make transactions transparent, but it cannot automatically establish copyright ownership.

Personally, I'd consider clear rights verification one of the most important foundations for real-world IP adoption.

If IPX gets this part right, it could address a problem that is often overlooked in conversations about tokenized entertainment.
